html:
"Paleo-Koreans" is the map's label for the people of the Korean Peninsula and southern Manchuria in 1500, 1000 and 700 BCE, before written records. What we know comes from archaeology.

These centuries are the Mumun or "plain pottery" period, named for its undecorated pots. It followed the comb-pattern pottery of the Jeulmun hunters and fishers. Mumun people grew rice in paddy fields and millet in dry fields and lived in villages of pit houses; later they also used bronze daggers and mirrors. They built many thousands of dolmens, stone burial tables, and Korea holds a large share of the world's dolmens.

In the north, the first state that Chinese records name, Gojoseon, grew out of this world. Its fall to the Han in 108 BCE opened the way to the Three Kingdoms.
